summary:
Washington stands under the United States federal framework on travel documents and entry screening, which applies in every state. Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, while X-marker passports issued before the change remain valid until expiry. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992; the Human Rights Campaign records the policy as still challenged in federal courts. The ACLU is litigating on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. An executive order of 5 February 2025 on women's sports was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes would be barred from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, with visa applicants flagged by an internal marking and any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth treated as fraud carrying a permanent bar. Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can out a trans traveller.

Washington's own law runs against the federal direction. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment names Washington among the most protective states and, with Colorado, Hawaii and Maryland, among those with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures; the same assessment records protections in Washington for people relocating from states with hostile law. Shield laws and executive orders adopted in Washington during the 2023 and 2024 batches are enforceable against out-of-state action, and the state appears on a nationwide tracker of such measures. Two Washington ballot initiatives on the November ballot are flagged by that assessment as targeting transgender residents.

Custody in Washington is a documented site of both obligation and sanction. In October 2023, under court order and rulings, Washington state prisons were legally required to provide gender-affirming healthcare and, where court-ordered, reassignment surgery to inmates. In July 2024 a trans woman prisoner was transferred from the women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison, placing birth-sex housing directly in use as a disciplinary measure.
tangentialFactors:
The protections described above sit inside a national pattern moving the other way. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings cover 9 states and 1 territory; in some of those states trans use of such facilities is a criminal offence. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, described by rights groups as a template for other legislatures. Conditions for changing a gender marker on a Washington licence or birth certificate differ from state to state across the country.

Federal restrictions on care and custody apply inside Washington as elsewhere. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes; proposed health-department rules in October 2025 would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18; and in July 2025 specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline were shut down. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates mandating short hair, withdrawal of hormone medication and substitution of psychiatric treatment, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would be treated "like a man," and refusal brought beatings and solitary confinement alongside widely reported sexual abuse.

Enforcement machinery has been turned on trans advocacy itself. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups, and a May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist. Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.
localsOnly:
Washington residents are covered by state health-insurance laws that the July 2026 assessment places in a small group, alongside Colorado, Hawaii and Maryland, requiring coverage of facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures. The state's shield laws and executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches operate against out-of-state action, meaning Washington can refuse compliance with investigative, legal or medical demands originating in states with bans, and residents returning from care obtained in Washington are protected on that basis. The same assessment records protections for people who move to Washington from states with hostile law.

Inside state prisons, the October 2023 court-ordered obligation to provide gender-affirming healthcare and reassignment surgery remains the legal standard, though the July 2024 transfer of a trans woman from the women's prison to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate shows that birth-sex housing is still imposed as a sanction in practice. Two ballot initiatives before Washington voters in November are flagged as targeting transgender residents, and their outcome will change the resident-facing position.

Whether Washington's 2023 and 2024 shield laws and executive orders have been amended, narrowed or expanded since those batches is not sourced in this inventory; the nationwide tracker listing is cited without a retrieval date.

The statutes and case citations underlying the October 2023 prison healthcare obligation are given only as "court order and rulings" in the source, without case names, and the current compliance position of the Washington Department of Corrections is unresolved.

Washington's rules for changing a gender marker on a state driver's licence or birth certificate are described in the inventory only indirectly, through a comparison showing that conditions differ state by state; the Washington-specific procedure is not sourced.
